items.title: Why Kerala is facing power cuts, and why the crisis has become a political fight
items.summary: Follow TNM’s WhatsApp channel for news updates and story links. Kerala's power crisis has now moved beyond an inconvenience for households and businesses to a political fight over a more fundamental question: why does the state repeatedly find itself short of electricity when demand rises or hydel generation falls? Partial power cuts have continued for nearly two weeks, with outages being imposed during evening peak hours and reports from several parts of the state of multiple cuts extending into the night. The disruption has hit students, families with young children, and people working from home, while the lack of advance information about some outages has added to public anger. The government has now said it will put in place a system to alert consumers about planned restrictions at the feeder level. The crisis has also exposed Kerala’s dependence on electricity purchased from outside the state. Electricity Minister Sunny Joseph has said Kerala can generate only around 25% of the electricity it consumes, with the rest coming from the central grid and power purchase agreements with generators outside the state. Its dependence becomes particularly acute when domestic hydel generation falls and electricity is not readily available through the power markets. The Congress-led United Democratic Front (UDF) government has blamed a combination of sharply increased demand, unusually high temperatures, inadequate rainfall, reduced inflows into reservoirs, and a shortage of power available nationally. Sunny Joseph has said peak demand, which was around 4,000 MW during the same period last year, has risen to about 5,200 MW. The peak period has also stretched beyond the traditional 7 pm to 10 pm window, with demand remaining high beyond 11 pm. Chief Minister V D Satheesan has also pointed to reduced inflow into reservoirs and the rise in peak-hour consumption, and said on September 9 that the government was working to bring in additional power and resolve the immediate shortage by around September 15. But that target has since been thrown into question , after KSEB chairman MG Rajamanickam indicated that restrictions could continue until the end of September, with sufficient additional power expected to become available from October 1 through short-term arrangements. items.summary: Follow TNM's WhatsApp channel for news updates and story links. A group of activists in Telangana monitoring the ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise have flagged several concerns with the notice phase. The draft electoral roll for Telangana was published on August 17, and the period for issuing notices began immediately and will continue until November 5. The final electoral roll will be published on November 11. In a representation to Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and Telangana Chief Electoral Officer (CEO) C Sudharshan Reddy, the activists said there was a lack of transparency in the SIR notices and hearings. They said there was no mechanism to check the current status of those who had been issued notices, and that notices were being issued without the application of mind in cases involving ‘logical discrepancies’. People across Telangana have started receiving notices for different reasons, such as non-mapping with the 2002 SIR, name mismatch, father’s or mother’s name mismatch, or unusual age differences flagged as logical discrepancies. Those who receive such notices have been asked to appear for hearings along with the required documents. The Election Commission also has an option to submit documents online in response to the notices. The letter noted that most of the SIR notices have given vague reasons such as “not mapped”, “name mismatched”, “father’s name mismatched”, “age difference”, etc., without providing precise details about the nature of the mismatch or discrepancy. Without exact information, people may not know what exactly they are required to prove, the activists said. They also said there must be a separate, clear list of documents or evidence required for each category. They also said that those who appear for the hearings do not have access to the details uploaded by the Booth Level Officer (BLO) on the ECI’s app, and have no way to track whether their documents have been accepted. This leaves people uncertain and requires them to wait for the final electoral roll to be published to know whether they have been excluded because of an unsatisfactory submission, while leaving them with no chance to rectify any issues, the letter said. items.summary: Wild Tamil Nadu , an hour-long documentary directed by Kalyan Varma, is a love story of sorts, narrated with nuance and put together with deep respect for the creatures filmed. A tribute to Tamil Nadu and its unique landscape as referenced in Sangam literature — Kurunji (the mountains), Mullai (forests), Marutam (crop land and rivers), Neidhal (seashore) and Paalai (desert), it is now playing in select PVR screens. Kalyan, who earlier co-directed Wild Karnataka , is an award-winning documentary filmmaker. What makes Wild Tamil Nadu fascinating is how much you take back from it. Creatures, some big but many small, shine under the spotlight. The documentary is produced by Arathi Krishna of Sundaram Fasteners. Director Kalyan Varma Music by Ricky Kej, which primarily features Indian sounds, lifts the experience, while editor Akhilesh Thambe manages to compress hours of footage into a memorable, even action-packed, 60 minutes. Actor Arvind Swami lends his rich voice for both the Tamil and English versions. In an interview with TNM, director Kalyan speaks of what went into the making of the documentary, how he likes to showcase wildlife and some of the creative choices exercised. That is one of the reasons why the big animals — elephants and the big cats — get little screen time. Instead, we consciously focussed on antlions, goby fish, the baya weaver and rock agama. items.title: What the Justice Ismail Commission actually says about MK Stalin and MISA
items.summary: In the Tamil Nadu Assembly on September 7, Chief Minister C Joseph Vijay wanted to talk about decorum. He was making a point about political inheritance — “take the good from the old politics, leave the bad.” In the same speech, he also levelled corruption allegations against the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK), reaching back to the 1978 Sarkaria Commission findings on alleged tender irregularities during the Karunanidhi years, and to more recent allegations related to TASMAC and municipal administration, which led to Enforcement Directorate investigations against DMK chief MK Stalin, Udhayanidhi Stalin, and V Senthil Balaji. He also spoke disparagingly about the incarceration of DMK leaders under the the Maintenance of Internal Security Act, 1971, or MISA, during the Emergency era. “Whatever we talk about, our friends keep saying we saw MISA, we saw MISA. All of us know the history of MISA very well.” He made the jaw gesture that had, by then, become a kind of shorthand of its own. The DMK and other parties immediately alleged that the gesture referred to how Stalin’s face was deformed during his MISA detention, an allegation that the CM denied. MISA was the law under which Indira Gandhi's government detained political opponents without trial during the Emergency. Under Section 3 of the Act, the Union or state government could order a person's detention if it was satisfied that this was necessary to prevent them from acting in ways prejudicial to the security of India, the security of the state, public order, or essential supplies and services. In Tamil Nadu, the DMK bore the brunt of such political detentions, with over 400 of its members jailed under it in 1976 alone. Stalin, then a young DMK legislator, was among those detenus, lodged in Madras Central Prison's ninth block in February 1976, where, as the Ismail Commission later found, he and others were beaten on the orders of the jail’s Superintendent and jailer. TVK’s minister for power CTR Nirmal Kumar went further, insinuating that Stalin’s arrest was for something else. “Under MISA, people had been arrested for theft, for robbery, for offences concerning women. It could not be assumed that everyone swept up during those months in 1976 had been arrested because of MISA. There were other reasons,” he said. items.title: Nearly 25% in Srikakulam’s Uddanam screened so far have kidney disease: Study
items.summary: Nearly one in four people screened so far in Andhra Pradesh’s Uddanam region have been found to have kidney disease, according to an interim analysis of an ongoing study aimed at identifying the causes of the region’s long-running kidney disease crisis. Of the 3,897 people screened so far, 949, or 24.35%, were found to have kidney disease, The Hindu reported. Of these, 550 were diagnosed with chronic kidney disease (CKD), while 399 were found to have chronic kidney disease of unknown aetiology (CKDu), according to an official statement issued on Saturday, September 12. The findings were presented to state Health Minister Satya Kumar Yadav by the team of experts conducting the study. Uddanam, a cluster of villages in the Srikakulam district of north coastal Andhra Pradesh, has for decades reported unusually high levels of kidney disease and deaths linked to renal failure. The problem has been documented since the early 1990s and has previously prompted studies by several institutions, including the Indian Council of Medical Research and Andhra University Medical College. A 2017 report said at least 4,500 people in the region had died from kidney-related ailments since 2005. The causes of the disease, particularly CKDu, have remained a subject of investigation. Previous research has examined possible environmental and occupational factors, including drinking water quality, pesticide exposure and agricultural work. Researchers have also investigated groundwater for heavy metals. However, no single cause has been conclusively established. The current study aims to screen 5,851 people across the Uddanam region and has so far covered four mandals. Kaviti mandal recorded the highest number and proportion of CKD and CKDu cases. Researchers said the findings warrant closer examination of environmental, occupational and other factors prevalent in the mandal. The interim analysis is based only on the people screened so far. The remaining participants will be screened shortly, after which the findings will be analysed alongside environmental and biomarker data before firm conclusions are drawn, researchers said. items.title: Telangana Assembly passes CURE Bill replacing 1955 GHMC Act
items.summary: Follow TNM's WhatsApp channel for news updates and story links. The Telangana Core Urban Region (Integrated Governance) Bill, 2026 (CURE Bill) was passed by the Assembly on September 12, Saturday. The Bill replaces the Greater Hyderabad Municipal Corporation (GHMC) Act, 1955, and establishes a unified governance framework for Hyderabad’s Core Urban Region (CURE), which currently includes three municipal corporations — the Greater Hyderabad Municipal Corporation, Cyberabad Municipal Corporation, and Malkajgiri Municipal Corporation. A draft of the CURE Bill was released for public consultation earlier on July 5. The Bill was passed with an amendment that reduces the maximum proposed annual increase in property tax to 10% from the 20% hike proposed in the draft. One of the biggest changes under the CURE Bill is the proposed shift in how property tax is assessed. The existing Annual Rental Value (ARV) system will be replaced by a Capital Value System (CVS), under which property tax will be linked to the government's market value of the property — the value used for registration purposes. Since these market values are generally much higher than the rental values that have remained largely unchanged for years, the shift to CVS is expected to considerably increase the property tax payable by many owners. The Bill says the revised tax will be introduced gradually for existing buildings, so the immediate financial burden can be reduced. The maximum annual hike has now been capped at 10%, with the tax expected to increase gradually until the CVS is fully adopted. Once the CVS is implemented, residential buildings will be taxed at 0.15% of their capital value, while non-residential buildings will be taxed at 0.75%. The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) opposed the Bill in the Assembly, while All India Majlis-e-Ittehadul Muslimeen (AIMIM) floor leader Akbaruddin Owaisi asked the Speaker to refer it to a select committee. Both the BJP and AIMIM raised concerns that the new system could lead to steep increases in property taxes. They also expressed concerns that the powers of CURE Apex Governance Council, headed by the Chief Minister, could supersede those of the Mayor and other elected municipal representatives.
